rule: A checkov pass proves DECLARED state — what the committed infrastructure definitions say the system will be — never account state. Each entry admits one checkov rule id from the pinned image and files it under exactly one KSI with the reviewer's reason; a rule the crosswalk does not carry is not judged, and a rule that moves between checkov versions fails checkov-crosswalk.test.ts against the vendored rule list. Every derived recipe evaluates the same checkov-results.json as iac-baseline-clean and asserts `count_eq 0` over the failed checks whose id it carries; a run in which none of a recipe's rules was evaluated gets no observation for that recipe and stays unevidenced (Guard), because an empty result over rules that never applied is not a clean result. The rows carry `proves: declared-state` and the register prints `declared` beside them so an assessor sees what kind of claim it is. Distinctness (docs/PLAN-REACH.md ground rule 3): declared state and account state are two planes, so a checkov row beside a runner or Prowler row on one KSI is two planes; two derived rows over the same checkov-results.json are one observation, and the reach ladder counts them as one toward the floor. Not a rename table and not exhaustive: the pinned image carries 1,179 rules over these three frameworks and this file admits the ones whose subject is the KSI's; adding a rule is a reviewed change with its basis written out.

rows.evidence: The committed infrastructure definitions declare no security group, network ACL, peering route or container port that admits unrestricted inbound or outbound traffic, at the scanned commit

plain.checks: Reads the network rules written into the committed infrastructure — security groups, network ACLs, peering routes and container images — and counts the ones that open a port to the whole internet or let everything out.
plain.violation: Some definition admits the internet to an administrative or web port, lets any destination out, or peers two networks without limit. It is what the code says the network will be, before anything is deployed; a running account may differ, and this check cannot see that.
plain.fix: Narrow the offending rule to the sources and ports the service needs, or remove it. Each failed check names the file, the resource and the rule, so the change is one line in one definition; a rule that must stay open belongs in a recorded decision.

rows.caveats: Declared state only: what the committed Terraform, Dockerfiles and workflows say, never what the account runs. A rule added by hand in the console, or a definition never applied, is invisible here. Corroborates the cloud plane; does not replace it.

rows.evidence: The committed infrastructure definitions declare no publicly reachable data store, function or snapshot, no default public addressing, no root container user, and no injectable or over-permissioned workflow, at the scanned commit

plain.checks: Reads the committed infrastructure for anything that widens what an attacker can reach: resources exposed to the internet, subnets that hand out public addresses, containers that run as root, and workflow steps that can be injected or that hold write-all permissions.
plain.violation: Something in the definitions is reachable, writable or privileged beyond what its job needs, and a compromise of it has somewhere to go next. It is the declared shape of the system, not a measurement of the running one.
plain.fix: Make the resource private, give the container a user, scope the workflow token, or fix the interpolated step. Every failed check names the file and the setting; exposure that is intended belongs in a recorded decision, not a silenced rule.

rows.caveats: Declared state only. Public exposure created outside the committed definitions, and lateral-movement paths through data rather than configuration, are not seen. Corroborates the cloud plane; does not replace it.

rows.evidence: The committed infrastructure definitions place workloads inside VPCs, attach every security group and network ACL to something, avoid platform defaults, and describe every rule, at the scanned commit

plain.checks: Reads the committed infrastructure for whether the logical network is actually used: whether functions, clusters and databases sit inside a VPC, whether the security groups and ACLs written down are attached to anything, and whether default networks and undescribed rules are avoided.
plain.violation: A workload sits outside the network's controls, a control exists but guards nothing, or the platform's defaults stand in for a design. The flow controls the definitions were meant to enforce are not enforcing anything for that resource.
plain.fix: Move the resource into the VPC, attach the orphaned group or ACL, replace the default with a defined network, or add the description the review needs. Each failed check names the resource; the change is in that definition.

rows.caveats: Declared state only: the network as written, not as routed. Whether traffic actually flows the way the definitions intend is the cloud plane's question.

rows.evidence: The committed infrastructure definitions authenticate databases through IAM, give instances a role rather than a key, and grant no policy that exposes credentials, at the scanned commit

plain.checks: Reads the committed infrastructure for how services prove who they are to each other: databases that accept IAM identities instead of passwords, instances that carry a role instead of a key, and policies that would let a service read or mint another's credentials.
plain.violation: A service authenticates with a shared secret where an identity-based method was available, or a policy lets one service reach into another's credentials. It is the declared arrangement; a secret rotated by hand outside the definitions is not visible here.
plain.fix: Enable IAM authentication on the store, attach a role to the instance, and cut the credential-exposing actions from the policy. Each failed check names the resource; a service that genuinely needs a static secret belongs in a recorded decision with its rotation stated.

rows.caveats: Declared state only, and narrow: the rules cover databases, instances and IAM policies, not every service-to-service path. Corroborates the cloud plane and the secrets checks; does not replace either.

rows.evidence: The committed infrastructure definitions enable logging on every resource whose definition carries a logging switch — buckets, gateways, load balancers, clusters, VPCs, firewalls and databases — at the scanned commit

plain.checks: Reads the committed infrastructure for every resource whose definition has a logging switch — storage buckets, API gateways, load balancers, clusters, VPC flow logs, firewalls, databases — and counts the ones where it is off.
plain.violation: A resource is defined with its logging disabled, so the events it would produce never exist to be listed, monitored or audited. It is the definition that is silent; whether a running resource was later switched on by hand is not visible here.
plain.fix: Turn the logging setting on in the definition and point it at the destination the rest of the logs use. Each failed check names the resource and the setting; a resource whose logs are genuinely not wanted belongs in a recorded decision.

rows.caveats: Declared state only, and only for resources whose definition carries a logging switch. Application-level events and anything enabled outside the definitions are not seen. Corroborates the cloud plane; does not replace it.

rows.evidence: The committed infrastructure definitions declare an enabled, all-region, validated and encrypted CloudTrail delivered to CloudWatch Logs, with log groups retained for at least a year, at the scanned commit

plain.checks: Reads the committed infrastructure for the central audit feed: whether an account-wide trail is defined, whether it covers every region and delivers to a central log store, whether its files are validated and encrypted, and whether log groups keep records long enough.
plain.violation: The central feed is missing, partial, unencrypted, unvalidated or short-lived in the definitions, so the record a security team would search is either not being written centrally or could be altered without notice. It is what the code declares, not what the account is doing today.
plain.fix: Define the trail with all regions, log file validation, a customer-managed key and a CloudWatch Logs destination, and set retention on the log groups. Each failed check names the resource and the missing setting.

rows.caveats: Declared state only. A trail created outside the definitions, and the SIEM itself, are not seen — this is the feed's declaration, not the system that reads it. Corroborates the cloud plane; does not replace it.

rows.evidence: The committed infrastructure definitions declare backups, point-in-time recovery, retention, versioning, deletion protection and failover on every data store whose definition carries them, at the scanned commit

plain.checks: Reads the committed infrastructure for every data store — databases, caches, tables, volumes, file systems, buckets — and counts the ones defined without a backup, without point-in-time recovery, with too short a retention, or without the deletion protection and standby that a recovery objective depends on.
plain.violation: A store is defined in a way that cannot meet a recovery objective: nothing backs it up, the backup does not reach back far enough, or one call can delete it. It is the declared arrangement; whether a backup was ever restored is a different question this check does not answer.
plain.fix: Add the store to a backup plan or enable its backup setting, lengthen retention to the objective, and turn on deletion protection and failover. Each failed check names the resource; the objectives themselves live in the recovery plan, not here.

rows.caveats: Declared state only, and the objectives are not read: this shows backups exist as defined, not that they align with a stated recovery point or time. Restore testing is the cloud plane's and the plan's. Corroborates; does not replace.

rows.evidence: The committed infrastructure definitions encrypt every store, volume, queue, stream and secret at rest, accept only TLS on every listener and endpoint, and keep their keys enabled and scoped, at the scanned commit

plain.checks: Reads the committed infrastructure for encryption in both directions: whether each store, volume, queue, stream and secret is defined with encryption at rest, whether each listener, distribution and endpoint refuses plaintext and old TLS, and whether the keys behind them are enabled and not open to every principal.
plain.violation: Some definition holds or moves information without encryption, or rests on a key whose control has been given away. It is what the code declares; encryption switched on later by hand, or data outside these resources, is not seen.
plain.fix: Enable encryption at rest on the resource, require TLS on the listener, raise the TLS policy, and tighten the key policy. Each failed check names the resource and the setting; where a customer-managed key is asked for and a platform key is deliberate, record the decision.

rows.caveats: Declared state only. Whether the key material is managed well, and whether data in transit inside a private network is protected, are beyond these rules. Corroborates the cloud plane; does not replace it.

rows.evidence: The committed container images disable certificate validation for no download, package manager or language runtime, at the scanned commit

plain.checks: Reads the committed container image definitions for build steps that switch off certificate checking — for curl and wget, for pip, npm, yarn and git, for the package managers, and through the environment variables the runtimes honour.
plain.violation: A build step will accept any server as the one it meant to reach, so whatever it downloads could have come from anywhere on the path. The image is built that way every time; it is the declared build, not a measurement of a running container.
plain.fix: Remove the flag or variable that disables validation and install the certificate the build actually needs. Each failed check names the file and the instruction; a private authority belongs in the image's trust store, not in a switch that trusts everyone.

rows.caveats: Declared state only, and container images only: validation disabled at runtime, or in application code, is not seen here. Corroborates the cloud plane's session-authenticity checks; does not replace them.
